You've heard about the Amazon data centers where residents have reported clusters of rare cancers and miscarriages and where wastewater containing nitrates is sprayed onto farmlands.

It smells like gas outside. And you've seen the George Mason study confirming that data centers pose health risks through air pollution, water contamination, noise, and rising energy costs.

Now, I don't need to convince you. You're already the kind of leaders who pay attention. So instead of repeating what you already know, let me tell you what developers want. The technology inside these buildings will be obsolete before the concrete dries.

A hedge fund manager thought these facilities lasted 10 years. Experts told him 3 to 10 at the very most. Because new chips come out every year or two, and they make the old ones obsolete. Cooling systems change.
Power requirements change. The buildings can't keep up. Mountain Road will take years to build. By the time the last building goes up, the first building's guts are outdated. That's not a tax base.
That's a stranded asset. And while a data center takes 18 to 24 months to build, the power infrastructure takes five to 10 years. Transformers are backordered for four years. The grid can't keep up.

So what happens when the technology moves on before the power even arrives? You have a chance to do what the Planning Commission already did. In January, they looked at Hunting Hawk. They heard the residents. They voted no, Hanover is not for sale.
So now it's gonna be your turn soon. Virginia gives up 1.6 billion a year in tax breaks to this industry. Families in Loudoun pay over $100 more each year to subsidize grid upgrades.

When Mountain Road comes in May, vote no. The Planning Commission showed courage with Hunting Hawk. Now it's your turn. And consider something bolder. Senator Bernie Sanders, and no matter your politics, You have to respect someone who fights for working families.
Just called for a national moratorium. 11 states have introduced moratorium legislation this year. Virginia is the data center capital of the world. We can afford to pause.

And what's more, we can afford to lead. So protect the people that live here. Protect their wallets. Protect their water. Protect the land that makes Hanover feel like nowhere else, like what was said earlier, that is beautiful Hanover.

So please, be the heroes of Hanover. Vote no. Protect us. Thank you very much. Thank you, ma'am. Next speaker, please. Please come forward, state your name, the district that you live, or the entity that you represent.

Thank you for being with us. Hi, Shannon Todd, Mechanicsville District. Good evening, supervisors, and thank you for the opportunity to speak tonight. I'm asking you to oppose, or at least pause, approval of any hyperscale data center until we have firm protections for Hanover's taxpayers, our electric grid, and our water.

This vote is not about being pro-business versus anti-business. It is about being pro-Hanover and pro-responsible planning. These trillion-dollar corporations are abusing permits, demanding more energy and water, and shifting enormous risks onto local communities.

We see this clearly in many communities around the country. Across the country, we are seeing a clear pattern. Once these hyperscale AI data centers are built, the companies come back demanding more power, water, turbines, and generators, far beyond what was initially sold to local leaders.

Example number one, Elon Musk with XAI in South Memphis, Tennessee. He installed and operated dozens of methane turbines before receiving any permits from the Clean Air Act. After obtaining a permit to run 15 turbines, thermal imagery shows he is running at least 35.

There has been an increase in asthma-related ambulance calls in this area since then. Example number two, Metta's Hyperion AI Data Center in Louisiana. Regulators originally approved three gas plants for a 2,200-acre campus.

Metta quietly bought 1,400 more acres of land, set up a joint venture with Blue Owl Capital to fund it, and is now increasing its needs to 10 gas plants. This is a classic bait-and-switch to communities and meta-knows-how-to-play this game.

Example number three, Amazon Data Center is right here in Northern Virginia. We have seen an expansion far beyond what was originally projected. In 2019, it was estimated they will need 1,700 megawatts of power, but newer estimates show 2,700.

Dominion forecasts it will jump to 9,000 within the decade. Corporate can be greedy. A billion dollars is never enough for them. They do not have our residents' best interests at heart, and they never will because they don't live here. We're just numbers to them. But we are more than just numbers to you.

We are your neighbors, our children go to your schools, we go to church with you, and we run into you at the grocery store. And we have put our trust in you as our elected leaders. You are taking a gamble on your residents' health and well-being if you allow these data centers into our county.

If you lose, Hanover residents will pay the price. As of right now, you can prevent these same tragedies from happening in our own backyard. You made the choice when you took your oath of office to work for the people of Hanover County, and they are telling you no. Nobody in Hanover supports these data centers, and only you have the power to stop this before it's too late.

And now on behalf of the Hanover County Community Services Board, I want to voice our support for the proposed budget presented by our county administrator. Reflecting on my second year's chair, one thing is exceptionally clear. this work is essential and it's increasingly complex. In fiscal year 25, Hanover CSB served over 2,200 individuals in our core programming, including nearly 500 who relied on 24-7 crisis services. This year, the CSB expanded its impact through several key initiatives. We launched the Naloxone by Mail program and have distributed 1,059 boxes to Hanover County households since January of 2025. With the Regional Opioid Abatement Authority grant, we partnered with

their neighboring jurisdictions of Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield, and were able to hire hospital liaisons to connect pregnant and parenting women of substance-exposed infants to critical CSP services. We also partnered with 28 local employers, including Hanover County Human Resources, to create more jobs for individuals with disabilities. Concurrently, we're continuing to strengthen our core services that many in our community rely on daily. For the first time since COVID, the CSP secured two full-time prescribers to serve individuals across both behavioral health and developmental disability services. We also implemented the Marcus Alert program nine months ahead of schedule and did so in close partnership where there are excellent public safety and

emergency communications here in the county, improving response to behavioral health crisis in real time. This work saves lives. And it must be noted that these efforts are happening within the broader context of changes in society that are impossible to ignore. The demand for services continuously grows. Our community's needs are constantly evolving, becoming more complex every day. Our residents, while fortunate to live in Hanover and Myriad Ways, are not immune to the pressures found elsewhere in the world and are likewise experiencing increasing mental health challenges, ongoing barriers to housing, limited access to private providers for developmental

disability services, and the pain of far too many lives lost to suicide and overdose.
